text: Given an integer array, return the length of the longest turbulent subarray. A subarray is turbulent if the comparison sign flips between each pair of neighbors: bigger, smaller, bigger, and so on.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the subarray is contiguous. I look at each step between neighbors, and each step is either up or down. The steps must strictly alternate: up, down, up, or down, up, down. It can start either way. And if two neighbors are equal, that step is neither up nor down, so it breaks the run. Is that right?
Yes. Strict alternation, either direction, and equal neighbors break it.

Okay. Then a few small facts. One element alone always counts, so the answer is at least one. Any two different neighbors make a length-two run, one step. And the only thing that matters is the direction of each step, not how big it is. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The array has up to four times ten to the fourth elements, and each value is between zero and ten to the ninth.

Got it. So I want one pass. Values go up to ten to the ninth, which fits in an int — but I'll keep it in mind in case I ever multiply two differences. On the example, nine, four, two, ten, seven, eight, eight, one, nine, the best run is index one to five, four, two, ten, seven, eight: down, up, down, up, length five. It can't grow left, because nine to four is down again, and it can't grow right, because eight to eight is equal. The all-up example gives two, and a single one hundred gives one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach tries every start and grows each one until it breaks. That's quadratic — correct, and I'd keep it as a brute force to test against, but too slow at forty thousand elements. This problem reminds me of the two-running-Kadanes pattern: a running best ending at each index, kept as two coupled values that swap into each other. Here I keep two runs ending at index i — one whose last step goes up, one whose last step goes down. An up step can only extend a run that ended going down, and the other way around, so the two values feed each other.

Here's the plan. One: keep three numbers, all starting at one — the best length, the up run, and the down run ending here. Two: for each index from one, copy both runs first; an up step makes the up run previous-down plus one, a down step makes the down run previous-up plus one, and whichever direction this step is not resets to one. Equal steps reset both, for free. Three: refresh the best with both. One thing worth flagging — the start value is one, not zero. Starting the best at zero returns zero for a single element, and resetting to zero makes every run one short — example one would give four. A one-counter version works too, but comparing steps the easy way multiplies two differences, which can overflow. Two counters only compare. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Best, up, and down all start at one, and one loop from index one: save both runs as previous-up and previous-down, then set each with a ternary — greater-than gives previous-down plus one, less-than gives previous-up plus one, otherwise one — and take the max. One thing worth flagging — those copies are for correctness. If the second line reads the up run directly, it sees the value the first line just overwrote, which is one on every down step. So every down step cuts to two: example one returns three, and zero, one, zero returns two instead of three. Also, I never multiply neighboring differences — on zero, a billion, zero, that product overflows an int.

Let's dry-run the code with example one — expected five. The row that matters is index five: seven to eight goes up, so the up run becomes previous-down plus one, four plus one, five. That four came from index four, where ten to seven went down and took the up run's three. So the chain passes back and forth — two, three, four, five — for the run four, two, ten, seven, eight. Then eight to eight resets both to one, and nothing later beats five. That matches. Corner cases: all up gives two, since the down run stays at one. A single element gives one, because the loop never runs. Zero, one, zero gives three — the version without copies returns two. And four equal fives give one; using greater-or-equal would wrongly turn example one into six.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one pass, two compares and a max per step. Space is constant — a few integers. No early exit, so it's always n minus one steps, about twenty-eight microseconds at forty thousand elements. I only compare values, never do math on them, so there's no overflow. Oh, one more thing — I'd test this against the brute force. I ran over two hundred twenty-three thousand cases with zero mismatches. That matters here: the version without copies passes two of the three official examples, yet fails nineteen hundred twenty-three of about three thousand three hundred small arrays. Hand-picked tests can miss that; a brute-force check won't.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You split the state into two runs, last step up and last step down, and saw that they cross-feed: each one extends the other. You explained why the previous copies are a correctness need, not style — without them every down step cuts to two, and zero, one, zero breaks it. And you avoided the difference-product trick because it overflows an int at a billion. Good work.
